name: Interval Game
description: Alice and Bob are playing a game involving two intervals, $$$[l_1, r_1]$$$ and $$$[l_2, r_2]$$$, constrained by integers $$$x_1$$$ and $$$x_2$$$ respectively. The intervals satisfy $$$1 \le l_1 \le r_1 \le x_1$$$ and $$$1 \le l_2 \le r_2 \le x_2$$$. The game is played as follows. In one turn, a player must choose one of the two intervals (let's say the $$$i$$$-th interval $$$[l_i, r_i]$$$) and perform exactly one of the following operations: Replace $$$l_i$$$ with a strictly smaller integer $$$l'_i$$$ such that $$$1 \le l'_i \lt l_i$$$. Replace $$$r_i$$$ with a strictly larger integer $$$r'_i$$$ such that $$$r_i \lt r'_i \le x_i$$$. The player who cannot make a valid move loses the game. The game setup proceeds in two steps: First, Alice chooses the values of $$$l_1$$$ and $$$r_1$$$ to determine the first interval. It must be a valid interval within $$$[1, x_1]$$$. Then, the second interval $$$[l_2, r_2]$$$ is chosen uniformly at random from all possible valid intervals within $$$[1, x_2]$$$. Once the intervals are chosen, the game begins with Alice moving first . Assuming both Alice and Bob play optimally, Alice wants to choose the initial interval $$$[l_1, r_1]$$$ to maximize her probability of winning. Your task is to find such an interval. If there are multiple optimal intervals, you may output any one of them.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains two integers $$$x_1$$$ and $$$x_2$$$ ($$$1 \le x_1, x_2 \le 5 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the upper bounds for the two intervals. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$x_1$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$5 \cdot 10^5$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$x_2$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$5 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output two integers $$$l_1$$$ and $$$r_1$$$ ($$$1 \le l_1 \le r_1 \le x_1$$$) — the optimal interval chosen by Alice. If there are multiple optimal intervals, you may output any one of them.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2217F — Interval Game [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
